name: Meropenem
route_note: IV bolus or infusion every 8 hours; extended infusion used in critical care. Also combined with vaborbactam (Vabomere).

discovery.note: A 1-beta-methyl carbapenem that is stable to renal dehydropeptidase-I, so it does not need cilastatin.

tagline: Ultra-broad carbapenem reserved for serious and resistant Gram-negative infections
summary: Meropenem is a broad-spectrum carbapenem active against most Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, including ESBL- and AmpC-producing Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is a key hospital antibiotic whose effectiveness is threatened by carbapenemase-producing organisms.
mechanism: Meropenem binds multiple penicillin-binding proteins (especially PBP2 and PBP3 in Gram-negative bacteria), inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing rapid bactericidal lysis.

Its carbapenem nucleus and trans-hydroxyethyl side chain resist hydrolysis by nearly all serine beta-lactamases except carbapenemases (KPC, OXA-48-like) and the metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP). Its 1-beta-methyl group protects it from renal dehydropeptidase-I.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: The FDA approves meropenem (Merrem IV, AstraZeneca).

history.title: NDM-1
history.detail: New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase 1 is identified in a Klebsiella isolate from a patient treated in India (described 2009), later spreading worldwide.

history.title: WHO AWaRe classification
history.detail: WHO begins grouping antibiotics on its Essential Medicines List into Access, Watch and Reserve; meropenem is a Watch antibiotic.

history.title: Meropenem-vaborbactam
history.detail: The FDA approves meropenem-vaborbactam (Vabomere) for complicated urinary tract infections.

history.title: MERINO trial
history.detail: Meropenem outperforms piperacillin/tazobactam for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli and Klebsiella bloodstream infections.

pk.metabolism: minor hydrolysis to an inactive open-ring metabolite

serious: Severe reduction of valproate levels, risking breakthrough seizures

facts: Carbapenems lower serum valproate concentrations so markedly that co-administration is generally avoided.
Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales are on WHO's list of critical-priority pathogens.
